source.title: Sanctions Advisory for the Maritime Industry, Energy and Metals Sectors, and Related Communities

summary: GOLDEN LABEL, hand-drafted against the PDF. Joint State, OFAC and Coast Guard advisory on deceptive shipping practices used to move sanctioned petroleum, petrochemicals, metals, coal and sand for Iran, North Korea and Syria: disabling or spoofing AIS, painting over vessel names and IMO numbers, falsified bills of lading and certificates of origin, ship-to-ship transfers at sea, indirect routing and transshipment through third countries, false flags and flag hopping, and complex or shifting ownership and ISM management structures that hide the beneficial owner of cargo. Annex A is sector-by-sector due-diligence guidance; Annex B sets out the three sanctions programmes with UN Panel of Experts findings on North Korean coal and sand exports via STS transfers to barges in Chinese waters, refined petroleum deliveries far above the UNSCR 2397 cap, acquisition of scrap-bound vessels, and the Iran-Syria oil scheme settled through a payment offsetting arrangement that funded IRGC-QF, Hizballah and HAMAS.

citations.quote: vessels engaged in illicit activities may also intentionally disable their AIS transponders or manipulate the data transmitted in order to mask their movement.

STS transfers—especially at night or in areas determined to be high-risk for sanctions evasion or other illicit activity—are frequently used to evade sanctions by concealing the origin or destination of surreptitiously transferred petroleum, coal, and other material.
They may also repeatedly register with new flag states (“flag hopping”) to avoid detection.
North Korea is acquiring old vessels destined for scrapping and incorporating them into its fleet of vessels transporting coal and other goods.

Authorities have found that sanctions evaders have falsified shipping documentation pertaining to petrochemicals, petroleum, petroleum products, or metals (steel, iron) or sand in order to disguise their origin.
actors, such as Iran’s IRGC-QF, attempt to evade U.S. sanctions by obfuscating the origin, destination, and recipient of oil shipments.

Bad actors attempt to take advantage of this complexity through the use of complex business structures, including those involving shell companies and/or multiple levels of ownership and management, to disguise the ultimate beneficial owner of cargo or commodities in order to avoid sanctions or other enforcement action

Malign actors may attempt to disguise the ultimate destination or origin of cargo or recipients by using indirect routing, unscheduled detours, or transit or transshipment of cargo through third countries.
Bad actors also may engage in a pattern of changes in the ownership or management of companies or in the International Safety Management Code (ISM) management companies used.
situations where ownership of a vessel is transferred between companies controlled by the same beneficial owner and where there is no discernable legitimate purpose for the transfer.
summarizes several tactics utilized to facilitate sanctionable or illicit maritime trade linked to Iran, North Korea, and Syria.
Sensitizing clients to potential sanctions risk related to activities involving Iranian, North Korean, or Syrian ports.

typologies.label: AIS disablement and spoofing to mask vessel identity and movement

citations.quote: The practice of manipulating AIS data, referred to as “spoofing,” allows ships to broadcast a different name, International Maritime Organization (IMO) number
UNSCR 2397 (OP 13), which expresses concern that North Korea-associated vessels intentionally disregard requirements to operate AIS to evade UNSCR sanctions monitoring.

typologies.label: Ship-to-ship transfers at sea to conceal cargo origin or destination

citations.quote: are frequently used to evade sanctions by concealing the origin or destination of surreptitiously transferred petroleum, coal, and other material.
The majority of these exports have occurred via STS transfers from North Korea-flagged vessels to local barges in Chinese territorial sea.
North Korean ports received at least 221 tanker deliveries of refined petroleum, including at least 157 deliveries procured from illicit STS transfers involving North Korean vessels.
Bad actors may falsify the flag of their vessels to mask illicit trade.  They may also repeatedly register with new flag states (“flag hopping”) to avoid detection.
instances when a vessel has changed flags frequently in a short period of time in a suspicious manner consistent with flag hopping.

typologies.label: Physical alteration of vessel identification (painted-over names and IMO numbers)

citations.quote: Vessels involved in illicit activities have often painted over vessel names and IMO numbers to obscure their identities and pass themselves off as different vessels.
to use deceptive practices to hide their identities, including by using false vessel names or IMO numbers.

typologies.label: Payment offsetting arrangement settling sanctioned oil shipments

citations.quote: This scheme used a payment offsetting arrangement in which the sale and shipment of Iranian oil to Syria provided hundreds of millions of dollars to Iran’s terror proxy groups, including Hizballah, HAMAS, and the IRGC-QF.

extraction_notes: Golden label. SAN002 over PAT008 per the twin convention. AIS spoofing, STS transfers, flag hopping and painted-over identities are marked emergent as well as cited under SAN002: the library's SAN002 describes ownership and logistics networks, not the vessel-level deceptions this advisory is about, and each is a numbered tactic repeated across Annex A. Shell companies appear once (p3) so SAN004 is folded into SAN009. Below-market prices (p15) is a single red flag, not TBML002U. Falsified origin documents go to SAN006 not TBML005. Old-vessel acquisition and non-AIS barges (pp29-30) are cited under SAN002 rather than labelled. Payment offsetting (p35) kept emergent at low: one mention, but a settlement mechanism the library does not hold. Hizballah and HAMAS are proceeds recipients, the Government of Syria a sanctions target, neither labelled as actors. US is the designating state; Liberia, Panama and Marshall Islands are registry-compact members; none are jurisdictions.
